item.title: augmenting human intellect when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory. i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that wor...
item.description:
作者：Ryo Lu 账号：@ryolu_ 简介：Designed @Cursor_ai, @NotionHQ, @Stripe, built startups. I make a world where anyone can make software. Aspiring k-pop idol.
augmenting human intellect
when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory.
i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else.
the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it.
the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine.
he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system.
somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology.
more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening.
and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for.
i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined.
that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works?
sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work.
but not everything difficult is overhead.
sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question.
i want tools that leave room for that relationship.
in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach.
he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse.
not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard.
a system you can reshape as your understanding changes.
this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself.
the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller.
but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment.
i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us.
i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before.
what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission?
when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean.
not a world that no longer needs us. a world we have more ability to shape.

item.description:
作者：Peter Yang 账号：@petergyang 简介：Practical AI tutorials and interviews for busy people | Get my best AI skills and guides at https://t.co/6VAA6p81x6
I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long.
Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's.
But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries:
Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it.
Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing.
Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications.
📌 Watch my full Genie 4 tutorial to see how I created the worlds in the reel below: https://t.co/GvzPewT5gj

item.title: Can You Use AI To Make Good Art? — With Fred Graver
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18 The industry is in a tailspin. There are fewer opportunities for writers and producers and people who make things. And I really had the conviction that AI can help you figure out who you are, how you have to survive in this world, and also how to make things that will then promote you and promote your career.
Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:40 Depending on who you ask, right now is an apocalypse for creative people, or it's like the best time to be alive ever. I think it's it's one of the most important questions about AI as a technology. Can you use it to make good art, or can you only use it to make slop? That's why I'm extremely excited for this episode. My cohost Natalia Quintero interviewed Fred Graver.
Speaker 2 | 00:40 - 01:03 Fred is a four time Emmy award winning filmmaker and technologist who is using AI all the time to make really great stuff in film. And he came on to share how he uses it, how it can be used as a creative tool, and the dirty secret in Hollywood that a lot of people use it even if they won't admit to it. So Natalia, tell us about the conversation.
Speaker 3 | 01:04 - 01:20 It was so cool to talk to Fred and to learn from someone who's been a leader at the top of their industry for so many decades. And what's interesting is that Fred has actually done this a few times. He started his career as a Disney Imagineer.
Speaker 2 | 01:20 - 01:21 That's the coolest thing.
Speaker 3 | 01:21 - 02:02 Kind of the dream jobs. And then he, you know, built this incredible career at VH1 and MTV, and then he kind of threw it all away and became the head of TV at Twitter when it was a startup, and that didn't totally make sense. But he he had this really interesting thesis of wanting to get closer and closer to the audience, And now he's done it again. You know, he's basically built what will be compound producing and rebuilt the production process from the ground up using his decades of expertise, the... An Emmy award winning artist to do it all over again, and we all get to use his skills.
Speaker 3 | 02:03 - 02:06 So if you want to be a producer, now you can produce like Fred.
Speaker 2 | 02:06 - 02:09 I love it. It's a great episode. Let's dive in.
Speaker 3 | 02:21 - 02:37 So, Fred, thank you so much for being with us. And I wanna start by actually just maybe getting a little bit of background on your career and how you got here. This... Maybe let's start, at the top. You're a professional writer.
Speaker 3 | 02:37 - 02:39 Yes. How did you get into that?
Speaker 1 | 02:39 - 03:04 I came to New York, and, I could type over a 100 words a minute. And we are back in the day of of IBM Selectrics and printers copies and all of that. And I went to work, and, oh, and I knew how to copy edit. And I went to work at the National Lampoon. And I was hired there, because I could I could type and I could copy edit, and I wouldn't screw up the joke.
Speaker 1 | 03:04 - 03:18 So a bad copy editor would go, well, this isn't grammatically correct, and I would understand, no. That's the joke. And, I began editing, stuff at the National Lampoon and writing for the National Lampoon. So that's... Yes.
Speaker 1 | 03:18 - 03:45 That's how I got started, which which for for people who are watching, who are every... In the every audience, yes, your your technical skills count. They will often get you in the door, particularly to jump ahead. You know, the whole kind of you're gonna get replaced by somebody who knows how to use AI. People who understand what's happening under the hood, are going to be incredibly in demand, I think.
Speaker 1 | 03:45 - 04:09 So, I went to work from there for for David Letterman, for Late Night with David Letterman, and stayed there for a long time. It was a great gig. And then went to work for Norman Lear. In the seventies, Norman was the king of television. I think he had four or five hit shows in the top 10 of the Nielsen rankings at one time.
Speaker 1 | 04:09 - 04:26 And he also was socially aware and very smart, and he was doing some new things with television. And I got hired. I worked with him. It was incredible learning experience, which then translated into my being a comedy writer. And I worked for for Cheers and in Living Color, and then, I heard a modem.
Speaker 1 | 04:26 - 04:58 And the first time I heard a modem, which was actually in the eighties, I just went, okay. This changes everything. Everything's going to be on something on your desk, and you're going to be able to do everything yourself. And so my first kind of tech gig was I was working with the Disney Imagineers. And there was this effort back in the day with Mike Ovets and Jeffrey Katzenberg and those guys, and they were terrified.
Speaker 1 | 04:58 - 05:15 This is, like, the late nineties, early two thousands. They're terrified by the Internet. But, you know, they began putting real bets down on what is this thing gonna be. I was there, and I was at MTV Networks in the kind of early web days. And then I took another right turn.
Speaker 1 | 05:15 - 05:31 I got hired by Twitter. This would be late two thousands. Right? It's about the second year that Twitter was around. And the theory was if if famous people that people love, celebrities or TV shows, are on Twitter, then people will get on Twitter.
Speaker 1 | 05:31 - 05:52 And and that's the best advertising we could do. And so that was my job, was to get the bird and real use cases onto the screen. Probably best case that ever happened was the famous Ellen DeGeneres selfie. That was how many million dollar worth of advertising. I did that.
Speaker 1 | 05:53 - 06:24 And then I was doing some consulting and things, and somebody said to me, hey. There's this machine learning thing that's AI, and, the engineers don't understand how people talk, and and people don't know what to talk about when they get to the machine. And and I... So I became a conversation designer at Microsoft. I was literally scripting bots, and I was working with the AI teams.
Speaker 1 | 06:24 - 06:55 And it was it was weirdly fascinating because you're just dealing with this what's going to become AI, what's going to become this interface, and trying to figure out, you know, what will that conversation be. And, also, it is a conversation. I think what a lot of people... When they freak out about AI, and and they freak out about an enormous box of things instead of all the things that are inside, but they're kind of like... They they use it as a search engine or it gave me the wrong...
Speaker 1 | 06:55 - 07:02 And they don't realize, no, it's a relationship. I was doing that. I was writing... Then I... They moved me to writing presentations.
Speaker 1 | 07:02 - 07:38 Microsoft's great kind of secret sauce is they have decades of data about how people use their software. If you're United Airlines and people are calling in to do whatever they're going to do, can we have an AI bot? Can we have Copilot go through everything you... We already know from thirty years of you guys using software to help them solve their problem? And so I did that for for for quite a while writing these presentations saying, here's what AI is, and here's what it does, and and, here's your problems.
Speaker 1 | 07:38 - 07:43 And the solution to your problems, oddly enough, are Microsoft products.
Speaker 3 | 07:45 - 07:46 Of course they are.
Speaker 1 | 07:46 - 07:46 Of course they were.
Speaker 3 | 07:46 - 08:20 What's so interesting to me about your career though is that at every sort of major turning point, you kind of... You have turned towards technology as early as joining the Disney Imagineers, which at the time was revolutionary and the work that they did has been so revolutionary. What do you think has been the core insight that you've taken at every turn? Like, from the Imagineers, to, you know, you worked in, like, the the golden era of TV. Yeah.
Speaker 3 | 08:20 - 08:33 But you also turned from that to go ...

item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
Vercel CI solves the "AI coding bottleneck" via: ① Fast and stable infrastructure (faster work) ② Turborepo integration (less work) ③ Agentic CI
① is obvious. Your CI is slow, flaky, goes down. We solve that. We operate 20 worldwide clusters doing millions of microVMs per day.
② is less obvious, but very powerful. Turborepo was designed to intelligently skip and cache prior work. The graph of dependencies is computed, not written.
Ask your agent to migrate to @turborepo and start saving money and time. Even if you don't use us. But you should, it's really good.
③ is a game-changer. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚌𝚒 in the CLI is the first step, because now your agents can inspect, abort, trigger, replay CI. Vercel Agent can help optimize it. And this is just the start.
You can expect a lot of hooks and capabilities to make CI something far more intelligent, that can even capture the nuance and judgment an engineer would have ("Are those tests even worth running?")
Agentic CI is the future of how we ship software. Excited to build it with you all!

item.description:
作者：Aditya Agarwal 账号：@adityaag 简介：General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early Eng @facebook, CTO @Dropbox, Board @Flipkart | Optimist, Builder, Dad
This is a LP letter that we recently wrote with our lessons on spotting talent from a decade of investing at the frontier.
https://t.co/v1TnHjvAox
The most common thing you hear about early stage investing is that "It is 90% about the founder".
We agree but have always been unsatisfied by the lack of falsifiability, specificity, and repeatability of that statement.
What are the dimensions of excellence? How do they translate into companies?
It was a pleasure to collaborate with @gopalkraman on this.
